Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, ignorance is the forerunner in the attainment of unwholesome states, followed by shamelessness and lack of moral dread.
For one who is immersed in ignorance and lacks true knowledge, wrong view arises;
for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises.”
From wrong intention, wrong speech arises;
from wrong speech, wrong action arises;
from wrong action, wrong livelihood arises.
From wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises;
from wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises;
from wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
“Monks, knowledge is the forerunner for the attainment of wholesome states, with moral shame and moral dread following close behind.
For one who has reached knowledge, monks, a wise person, right view arises;
for one with right view, right intention arises.”
From right intention, right speech arises;
for one of right speech, right action arises;
for one of right action, right livelihood arises.
“For one of right livelihood, right effort arises;
for one of right effort, right mindfulness arises;
for one of right mindfulness, right concentration arises.”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.2 (SN 45.2, PTS SN v 2) 1.
The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga)
The Discourse on the Half:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life, namely: having good friends, having good companions, having good associates.
“Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!”
"Ānanda, this entire holy life consists of this: namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
For a monk who has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, it is to be expected that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path."
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good associates develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment;
he develops right intention dependent on seclusion... [and so forth].
He develops right speech … [and so on] … he develops right action … [and so on] … he develops right livelihood … [and so on].
He develops right effort …pe… he develops right mindfulness …pe… he develops right concentration,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
"In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good associates develops the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.
By this method, Ānanda, it should be understood that this entire holy life consists of this: having good friends, good companions, and good associates.
For, Ānanda, by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; those subject to aging..."
“Beings subject to aging are liberated from aging; beings subject to death are liberated from death;
beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
It is by this method, Ānanda, that it should be understood how this entire holy life consists in this: namely, good friendship, good companionship, and good fellowship.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.3 (SN 45.3, PTS SN v 3) 1.
The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga)
The Sāriputta Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this holy life is entirely comprised of this: namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
This holy life, Sāriputta, is entirely comprised of this: namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.”
"It is to be expected, Sāriputta, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
And how, Sāriputta, does a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?"
“Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu develops right view dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment….
He develops right concentration dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
It is in this way, Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good comrades develops the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.”
"It is by this method, Sāriputta, that it should be understood how this entire holy life consists in this: namely, having good friends, having good companions, and having good associates.
For, Sāriputta, by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging;
beings subject to death are freed from death; and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
Beings are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

It is by this method, Sāriputta, that it should be understood how this entire holy life consists of this: namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates. This was the third [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 45.4 (SN 45.4, PTS SN v 4) 1. The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga) The Discourse to the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell? And what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? "Brahmin, it is because of ignorance that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. It is because of ignorance that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. "But how, Master Gotama, does ignorance become the cause, how does it become the reason, for some beings to be reborn in a state of misery... or for some beings to be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? "Brahmin, when one has a mind accompanied by lust, one acts with bodily, verbal, and mental deeds that are accompanied by lust. Having acted thus, one accumulates kamma that is accompanied by lust. With the accumulation of kamma accompanied by lust, one is reborn in a state accompanied by lust. Being reborn there, one experiences pleasure and pain that are accompanied by lust. This, brahmin, is how ignorance becomes the cause, how it becomes the reason, for some beings to be reborn in a state of misery... or for some beings to be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. [The Blessed One then spoke in detail regarding the mind accompanied by hatred and the mind accompanied by delusion. "But how, Master Gotama, is it that ignorance ceases, how does it cease, so that with the cessation of ignorance, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery... or some beings are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? "Brahmin, when one has a mind free from lust, one acts with bodily, verbal, and mental deeds that are free from lust. Having acted thus, one accumulates kamma that is free from lust. With the accumulation of kamma free from lust, one is reborn in a state free from lust. Being reborn there, one experiences pleasure and pain that are free from lust. This, brahmin, is how ignorance ceases, how it ceases, so that with the cessation of ignorance, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery... or some beings are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One: "Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for life."
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
There he saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi departing from Sāvatthī in a chariot drawn by entirely white mares.
The horses were indeed white, yoked with white ornaments; the chariot was white, as were its trappings, the reins, the whip, the parasol, the turban, the garments, and the sandals;
and he was fanned with a white yak-tail whisk.
Seeing him, people said this:
"Truly, sirs, it is a divine vehicle!
Truly, sirs, it has the form of a divine vehicle!"
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Sāvatthī for alms.
There, Bhante, I saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi departing from Sāvatthī in an all-white chariot drawn by mares.
Indeed, the horses yoked were white, their ornaments were white, the chariot was white, the upholstery was white, and the reins were white.”
The whip-handle was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the garments were white, the sandals were white,
and he was being fanned with a white yak-tail fan.
When people saw him, they said this:
“Truly, sir, this is the Brahma-vehicle!
Truly, sir, this has the form of the Brahma-vehicle!
“Is it possible, venerable sir, to designate the Brahma-vehicle within this Dhamma and Discipline?”
“It is possible, Ānanda,” the Blessed One said.
“Indeed, Ānanda, this noble eightfold path is a designation for the Brahma-vehicle,
a designation for the Dhamma-vehicle, and a designation for the unsurpassed victory in battle.”
Right view, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, culminates in the removal of hatred, and culminates in the removal of delusion.
Right intention, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, culminates in the removal of hatred, and culminates in the removal of delusion.
Right speech, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, [culminates in the removal of hatred] ... [and] culminates in the removal of delusion.
Right action, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion.
Right livelihood, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion.
Right effort, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion.
Right mindfulness, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion.
Right concentration, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, culminates in the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion.
It is by this method, Ānanda, that it should be understood how this is a designation for this very Noble Eightfold Path.
“It is called the ‘Brahma-vehicle,’ it is called the ‘Dhamma-vehicle,’ and it is called the ‘supreme victory in battle.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“For one whose faith and wisdom,
and the teachings, are always yoked as a burden;
for whom conscience is the pole, and the mind is the yoke-tie;”
Mindfulness is the protective charioteer;
the chariot has virtue as its equipment,
meditation for its axle, and energy for its wheels.
Equanimity is the concentration of the burden;
non-desire is the protection.
Non-ill will and non-cruelty—
For whom seclusion is the weapon,
and patience the shield and armor—
he proceeds toward security from bondage.
This unsurpassed Brahma-vehicle has arisen within oneself; by means of it,
the wise depart from the world.
"Nothing but victory upon victory.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 45.5 (SN 45.5, PTS SN v 6)
1. The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga).
Discourse on Purpose (Kimatthiyasutta).
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, wanderers of other sects ask us:
'For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?'"
“Venerable sir, when we are asked this by those wanderers of other sects, we answer them thus:
‘Friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the full understanding of suffering.
Venerable sir, when we are asked this and answer in this way, do we speak in accordance with what the Blessed One has said?”
"And we do not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false; we explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate point of criticism or reproach can be found against us.
"Truly, monks, when questioned thus, by answering in this way you have spoken exactly as I would say."
And you have not misrepresented me with what is untrue; you have explained in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate point of criticism or reproach arises against me.
For the holy life is lived under me for the sake of the full understanding of suffering.
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you:
‘But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of this suffering?’—being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
‘There is, friends, a path; there is a way for the full understanding of this suffering.’”
"And what, bhikkhus, is the path, what is the way for the full understanding of this suffering?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view ... right concentration."
“Monks, this is the path, this is the way for the full understanding of this suffering.
Thus, monks, being asked by those wanderers of other sects, you should answer them in this way.
The fifth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.6 (SN 45.6, PTS SN v 7) 1. Avijjāvagga First Discourse to a Certain Bhikkhu At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when ignorance is present, what comes into being? With the arising of ignorance, what arises? When ignorance is absent, what does not come into being? With the cessation of ignorance, what ceases? When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When ignorance is present, volitional formations come into being; with the arising of ignorance, volitional formations arise. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When volitional formations are present, consciousness comes into being; with the arising of volitional formations, consciousness arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When consciousness is present, name-and-form comes into being; with the arising of consciousness, name-and-form arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When name-and-form is present, the six sense bases come into being; with the arising of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When the six sense bases are present, contact comes into being; with the arising of the six sense bases, contact arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When contact is present, feeling comes into being; with the arising of contact, feeling arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When feeling is present, craving comes into being; with the arising of feeling, craving arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When craving is present, clinging comes into being; with the arising of craving, clinging arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When clinging is present, existence comes into being; with the arising of clinging, existence arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When existence is present, birth comes into being; with the arising of existence, birth arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When birth is present, aging-and-death comes into being; with the arising of birth, aging-and-death arises. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When aging-and-death is present, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being; with the arising of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When aging-and-death is absent, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not come into being; with the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When birth is absent, aging-and-death does not come into being; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When existence is absent, birth does not come into being; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When clinging is absent, existence does not come into being; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When craving is absent, clinging does not come into being; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When feeling is absent, craving does not come into being; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When contact is absent, feeling does not come into being; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When the six sense bases are absent, contact does not come into being; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When name-and-form is absent, the six sense bases do not come into being; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When consciousness is absent, name-and-form does not come into being; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When volitional formations are absent, consciousness does not come into being; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. Then another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One that we learn: ‘When ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come into being; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When ignorance is present, volitional formations come into being; with the arising of ignorance, volitional formations arise. And so on, up to: ‘When birth is present, aging-and-death comes into being; with the arising of birth, aging-and-death arises. And so on, up to: ‘When ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come into being; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. And so on, up to: ‘When birth is absent, aging-and-death does not come into being; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is marvelous, Ānanda! How well this has been stated by you: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One... “Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding ignorance as it really is, and without making it utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—this would be impossible. But if someone were to say: ‘Having directly known and fully understood ignorance as it really is, and having made it utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—that is possible. “If anyone were to say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding volitional formations... consciousness... name-and-form... the six sense bases... contact... feeling... craving... clinging... existence... birth... aging-and-death as it really is, and without making them utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—this would be impossible. But if someone were to say: ‘Having directly known and fully understood aging-and-death as it really is, and having made it utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—that is possible. “Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding aging-and-death as it really is, and without making it utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—this would be impossible. But if someone were to say: ‘Having directly known and fully understood aging-and-death as it really is, and having made it utterly exhausted, one could here and now realize the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’—that is possible. At Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before]... Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said: ‘the holy life, the holy life.’"
“Venerable sir, what is the holy life, and what is the culmination of the holy life?
“Bhikkhu, this very Noble Eightfold Path is the holy life; that is to say:
right view … right concentration.”
“Bhikkhu, that which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—
this is the culmination of the holy life.
The sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.7 (SN 45.7, PTS SN v 8) 1. Avijjāvagga The Second Discourse to a Certain Bhikkhu At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when ignorance is present, what does it have as its condition? And how does the volitional formation conditioned by ignorance come to be? Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.8 (SN 45.8, PTS SN v 8) 1.
The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga)
The Vibhaṅga Sutta.
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Noble Eightfold Path; I will analyze it for you.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the noble eightfold path?
It is as follows: right view … right concentration.
And what, bhikkhus, is right view?”
“Bhikkhus, whatever is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—
this, bhikkhus, is called right view.
And what, bhikkhus, is right intention?”
“Monks, whatever is the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty—
this, monks, is called right intention.
And what, monks, is right speech?”
“Monks, whatever is the abstaining from false speech, the abstaining from malicious speech, the abstaining from harsh speech, and the abstaining from idle chatter—
this, monks, is called right speech.
And what, monks, is right action?”
“Monks, whatever is the abstaining from taking life, the abstaining from taking what is not given, and the abstaining from unchaste conduct—
this, monks, is called right action.
And what, monks, is right livelihood?”
"Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood—
this, monks, is called right livelihood.
And what, monks, is right effort?"
Here, monks, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire... for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states;
...he generates desire... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen—
this, monks, is called right effort.
And what, monks, is right mindfulness?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
this, monks, is called right mindfulness.
And what, monks, is right concentration?

Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences pleasure with the body.
“Having entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in happiness,

mindful and equanimous,’ and with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity—
this, monks, is called right concentration.”
The Eighth.

"Bhikkhus, just as it is impossible that a grain of rice or a grain of barley, when wrongly directed, would pierce the hand or foot or cause blood to flow when stepped upon by the hand or foot—this cannot happen."
For what reason?
Because of the wrong aim of the pig, monks.

"It is impossible that by developing the path he will shatter ignorance, give rise to true knowledge, and realize Nibbāna.
Why is that? Because his view, monks, is wrongly directed."

“Bhikkhus, just as it is possible that a rice husk or a barley husk, when properly aimed, might pierce the hand or the foot and draw blood when stepped upon by the hand or the foot—it is possible for this to happen.
Why is that? Because the husk was properly aimed.”

"In the same way, monks, it is indeed possible that a monk—with right-directed view and with right-directed development of the path—will pierce ignorance, arouse true knowledge, and realize Nibbāna. Why is that?
Because it is possible."
“Because of his right direction of view, bhikkhus.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu with a rightly directed view and a rightly directed development of the path shatter ignorance, arouse true knowledge, and realize Nibbāna?

“He develops right concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment….
It is in this way, monks, that a monk with rightly directed view and rightly directed development of the path pierces ignorance, gives rise to true knowledge, and realizes Nibbāna.
The ninth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 45.10 (SN 45.10, PTS SN v 11) 1. Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga) The Discourse to Nandiya (Nandiyasutta) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when ignorance is present, what comes into being? With the arising of ignorance, what arises? When ignorance is absent, what does not come into being? With the cessation of ignorance, what ceases? When this was said, the Venerable Nandiya said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One’s grace that I understand: ‘When ignorance is present, formations come into being; with the arising of ignorance, formations arise. When ignorance is absent, formations do not come into being; with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. “It is so, Nandiya, it is so! When ignorance is present, formations come into being; with the arising of ignorance, formations arise. When ignorance is absent, formations do not come into being; with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. “Venerable sir, it is through the Blessed One’s grace that I understand: ‘With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “It is so, Nandiya, it is so! With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases... [as above] ...Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. When this was said, the Venerable Nandiya said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “You are welcome, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed; live as one who is celibate. That was the Venerable Nandiya’s full admission. Then the Venerable Nandiya, alone and secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time attained that for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life, having realized it here and now for himself with direct knowledge, dwelt therein. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Nandiya became one of the arahants. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One, and so I have heard it.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the wanderer Nandiya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Nandiya said this to the Blessed One:
“How many things, Master Gotama, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna, have Nibbāna as their ultimate goal, and culminate in Nibbāna?

“Nandiya, these eight things, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna, have Nibbāna as their ultimate goal, and culminate in Nibbāna. Which eight? [The eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path].”
“Namely: right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
These eight qualities, Nandiya, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna, have Nibbāna as their final goal, and culminate in Nibbāna.
When this was said, the wanderer Nandiya addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The tenth.

Ignorance and the half-verse.
Sāriputta and the Brahmin;

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.11 (SN 45.11, PTS SN v 12) 2. Vihāravagga First Discourse on Dwellings “Monks, there are these four dwellings for a noble disciple. What four? The dwelling of one who has confidence; the dwelling of one who is conscientious; the dwelling of one who is learned; and the dwelling of one who dwells in the holy life. These, monks, are the four dwellings for a noble disciple.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, I wish to retire into seclusion for half a month.
I am not to be approached by anyone, except for one who brings me almsfood.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Consequently, no one approached the Blessed One except for the single person who brought him almsfood.
Then, at the end of that half-month, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I dwelt in a portion of the very same dwelling where I dwelt when I had first attained full enlightenment.”
Thus I understand:
"Feeling has wrong view as its condition;
feeling also has right view as its condition... [and so on].
There is feeling conditioned by wrong concentration;
there is feeling conditioned by right concentration;
there is feeling conditioned by desire.
There is feeling conditioned by applied thought;
there is feeling conditioned by perception;
when desire is not subsided, applied thought is not subsided, and perception is not subsided, there is also feeling conditioned by that.
“Desire has subsided, thought has subsided, perception has subsided, and there is feeling conditioned by that.
For the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, there is exertion; when that state has been reached, there is also feeling conditioned by that. Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 45.12 (SN 45.12, PTS SN v 13) 2. Vihāravagga Dutiyavihārasutta – The Second Discourse on Dwellings “Bhikkhus, there are these four dwellings for a noble disciple. What four? ‘I will be one who gains robes that are blameless and without blemish,’ this is the first dwelling for a noble disciple. ‘I will be one who gains almsfood that is blameless and without blemish,’ this is the second dwelling for a noble disciple. ‘I will be one who gains a resting place that is blameless and without blemish,’ this is the third dwelling for a noble disciple. ‘I will be one who gains medicinal requisites for the sick that are blameless and without blemish,’ this is the fourth dwelling for a noble disciple. These, bhikkhus, are the four dwellings for a noble disciple.”
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for three months.
I am not to be approached by anyone, except for one who brings me almsfood."
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Consequently, no one approached the Blessed One except for a single person bringing almsfood.
Then, at the end of those three months, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I dwelt in a portion of that very dwelling where I dwelt when I had first attained full enlightenment.”
Thus I understand:
"Feeling arises with wrong view as its condition;
feeling also arises with the subsiding of wrong view as its condition."
There is feeling conditioned by right view;
there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right view...
[and so on] ...there is feeling conditioned by wrong concentration.
There is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of wrong concentration, and there is feeling conditioned by right concentration;
there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right concentration;
and there is feeling conditioned by desire.
There is feeling conditioned by desire,
there is feeling conditioned by applied thought,
and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of applied thought.
There is feeling conditioned by perception;
there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of perception;
when desire is not subsided, and thought is not subsided, and perception is not subsided, there is feeling conditioned by that as well.
“Desire has subsided, thought has subsided, perception has subsided, and there is feeling conditioned by that;
for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, there is exertion, and when that state has been reached, there is also feeling conditioned by that.

Thus have I heard:

"Friend Ānanda, it is said: ‘Non-celibacy, non-celibacy.’"
“What, friend, is uncelibacy?
“Excellent, excellent, friend Bhadda!
Your inquiry is excellent, friend Bhadda; your intuition is excellent; your thorough questioning is admirable.”
For thus you ask, friend Bhadda:
“‘Non-celibacy, non-celibacy,’ friend Ānanda, it is said.
What now, friend, is non-celibacy?”’”
“Yes, friend.
“Indeed, friend, this very eightfold wrong path is uncelibacy, namely:
wrong view … [and so on] … wrong concentration.”

'Friend Ānanda, it is said: "the holy life, the holy life.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 45.20 (SN 45.20, PTS SN v 16) 2. Vihāravagga Tatiyakukkuṭārāmasutta (The Third Discourse on the Kukkuṭārāma) At Sāvatthī. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five hindrances. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five hindrances, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What, bhikkhus, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the hindrance of sensual desire? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on sensual desires: this is the gratification in sensual desires. That sensual desires are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in sensual desires. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for sensual desires: this is the escape from sensual desires. What, bhikkhus, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the hindrance of ill will? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on ill will: this is the gratification in ill will. That ill will is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in ill will. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for ill will: this is the escape from ill will. What, bhikkhus, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the hindrance of sloth and torpor? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on sloth and torpor: this is the gratification in sloth and torpor. That sloth and torpor are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in sloth and torpor. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for sloth and torpor: this is the escape from sloth and torpor. What, bhikkhus, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on restlessness and remorse: this is the gratification in restlessness and remorse. That restlessness and remorse are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in restlessness and remorse. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for restlessness and remorse: this is the escape from restlessness and remorse. What, bhikkhus, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the hindrance of doubt? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on doubt: this is the gratification in doubt. That doubt is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in doubt. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for doubt: this is the escape from doubt. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five hindrances, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The mind of one who is hindered by sensual desire does not incline toward ardor, commitment, and exertion; rather, it inclines toward the abandoning of the hindrance of sensual desire. The mind of one who is hindered by ill will does not incline toward ardor, commitment, and exertion; rather, it inclines toward the abandoning of the hindrance of ill will. The mind of one who is hindered by sloth and torpor does not incline toward ardor, commitment, and exertion; rather, it inclines toward the abandoning of the hindrance of sloth and torpor. The mind of one who is hindered by restlessness and remorse does not incline toward ardor, commitment, and exertion; rather, it inclines toward the abandoning of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse. The mind of one who is hindered by doubt does not incline toward ardor, commitment, and exertion; rather, it inclines toward the abandoning of the hindrance of doubt. Just as a bird, wherever it goes, carries its own wings with it, so too, when a noble disciple has abandoned these five hindrances, known as the corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and has separated himself from them, he attains the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

He dwells in that way. As he dwells thus, he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the corruptions of the mind. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the corruptions of the mind. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. The gratification in the case of painful feeling is the seeking of its cessation; the danger is its very nature of being painful; the escape is the contemplation of it as impermanent. The gratification in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the seclusion from the defilements that arise in dependence upon it; the danger is its impermanence; the escape is the contemplation of it as impermanent. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that in regard to these three feelings, by breaking through the conceit ‘I am,’ one makes an end of suffering in this very life? “Bhikkhu, when one knows and sees the origin of feeling as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is, then in regard to these three feelings, by breaking through the conceit ‘I am,’ one makes an end of suffering in this very life. Thus, bhikkhu, by knowing and seeing contact as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is, one knows and sees the origin of feeling as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that one knows and sees name-and-form as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is? “Bhikkhu, when one knows and sees consciousness as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is, then one knows and sees name-and-form as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is. Thus, bhikkhu, by knowing and seeing formations as they really are, and also their passing away as they really are, one knows and sees consciousness as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is. This, bhikkhu, is called the passing away of ignorance. By knowing and seeing ignorance as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is, one knows and sees formations as they really are, and also their passing away as they really are. By knowing and seeing formations as they really are, and also their passing away as they really are, one knows and sees consciousness as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is... [and so on, tracing back through name-and-form, the sixfold base, contact, and feeling] ...one knows and sees feeling as it really is, and also its passing away as it really is. Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.32 (SN 45.32, PTS SN v 23) 4. Paṭipattivagga Dutiyapaṭipattisutta: The Second Discourse on Practice “Monks, there are these two kinds of practice. What two? And what, monks, is the practice that does not lead to the cessation of the influxes? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from the obsession by sensual desire that has arisen. He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by sloth and torpor... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from the obsession by doubt that has arisen. This, monks, is called the practice that does not lead to the cessation of the influxes. And what, monks, is the practice that leads to the cessation of the influxes? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual desire, and he understands, as it really is, the escape from the obsession by sensual desire that has arisen. He dwells with a mind free from ill will... free from sloth and torpor... free from restlessness and remorse... free from doubt, and he understands, as it really is, the escape from the obsession by doubt that has arisen. This, monks, is called the practice that leads to the cessation of the influxes. These, monks, are the two kinds of practice.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.35 (SN 45.35, PTS SN v 25) 4. The Chapter on Practice The First Discourse on Asceticism “Monks, there are these four kinds of asceticism. What four? The asceticism of fewness of wishes, the asceticism of contentment, the asceticism of solitude, and the asceticism of exertion. And what, monks, is the asceticism of fewness of wishes? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is few in wishes, easy to support, easily satisfied with the requisites of life. This, monks, is called the asceticism of fewness of wishes. And what, monks, is the asceticism of contentment? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is content with whatever robe he receives, whatever almsfood he receives, whatever lodging he receives, and whatever medicinal requisites for the sick he receives. This, monks, is called the asceticism of contentment. And what, monks, is the asceticism of solitude? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells alone, withdrawn from society. This, monks, is called the asceticism of solitude. And what, monks, is the asceticism of exertion? Here, monks, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, for their non-decline, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. This, monks, is called the asceticism of exertion. These, monks, are the four kinds of asceticism.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.38 (SN 45.38, PTS SN v 26) 4. Paṭipattivagga Dutiyabrahmaññasutta (The Second Discourse on the Brahmin) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of brahmins. What four? The one who is a brahmin by birth but not by conduct; the one who is a brahmin by conduct but not by birth; the one who is neither a brahmin by birth nor by conduct; and the one who is a brahmin both by birth and by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one a brahmin by birth but not by conduct? Here, someone is born into a high clan, such as the Khattiyas, the Brahmins, or the Householders; he is well-born on both sides, of pure descent, unassailable and impeccable with respect to birth back through seven generations of ancestors, and he is not one who has entered the homeless life under the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is called one who is a brahmin by birth but not by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one a brahmin by conduct but not by birth? Here, someone is born into a low clan, such as the bamboo-workers, the wicker-workers, the chariot-makers, the hunters, the basket-makers, or the flower-scavengers; he is not well-born on both sides, of pure descent, unassailable and impeccable with respect to birth back through seven generations of ancestors, yet he has entered the homeless life under the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata and is possessed of the virtues dear to the Noble Ones. This is called one who is neither a brahmin by birth nor by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one a brahmin both by birth and by conduct? The Yoga Sutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four yogas. Which four?
The bond of sensual desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance—
these, monks, are the four bonds. For the direct knowledge,
full understanding, total destruction, and abandonment of these four bonds, monks, this noble eightfold path is to be developed.
The Second.

Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
The Discourse on Clinging:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging.
What are the four?
“Sensual clinging, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self—
these, monks, are the four kinds of clinging.
For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandoning of these four kinds of clinging, monks, this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.”
Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.174 (SN 45.174, PTS SN v 59) 14.
Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
The Discourse on the Ties:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ties. What four?”
Covetousness is a bodily tie; ill will is a bodily tie; adherence to rules and observances is a bodily tie; and dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth" is a bodily tie.
These, monks, are the four ties.
For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandoning of these four ties, monks, this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.175 (SN 45.175, PTS SN v 60) 14.
Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
Which seven?”

The underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance—these, monks, are the seven underlying tendencies.

For the direct knowledge of these seven underlying tendencies, for their full understanding, for their destruction, and for their abandonment... [as before] ...this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.”
Fifth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.176 (SN 45.176, PTS SN v 60) 14.
The Chapter on Floods (Oghavagga)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?”
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … [as before] … odors cognizable by the nose … [as before] … tastes cognizable by the tongue … [as before] …
“Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—these, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
For the direct knowledge of these five cords of sensual pleasure, for their full understanding, for their destruction, and for their abandonment... this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.”
The Sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 45.177 (SN 45.177, PTS SN v 60) 14.
Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
The Discourse on the Hindrances:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances.
Which five?”

The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt—these, monks, are the five hindrances.
For the direct knowledge of these five hindrances, for their full understanding, for their destruction, and for their abandonment... [as before] ...this noble eightfold path is to be developed.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.178 (SN 45.178, PTS SN v 60) 14.
Oghavagga (The Flood Chapter)
The Discourse on the Aggregates of Clinging: “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates of clinging.
Which five?

That is to say: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
These, monks, are the five aggregates subject to clinging.

For the direct knowledge of these five aggregates subject to clinging, for their full understanding, for their destruction, and for their abandonment... [as before] ...this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.

Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
The Discourse on the Lower Fetters: “Bhikkhus, there are these five lower fetters.
Which five?”
“Bhikkhus, these are the five lower fetters: personality view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.
For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandonment of these five lower fetters, bhikkhus, this Noble Eightfold Path is to be developed.”
Ninth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.180 (SN 45.180, PTS SN v 61) 14.
Oghavagga (The Chapter on Floods)
The Discourse on the Higher Fetters: “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters.
What are the five?”
Sensual lust for the form realm, sensual lust for the formless realm,
conceit, restlessness, and ignorance— these, monks, are the five higher fetters. For the direct knowledge,
full understanding, exhaustion, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, the noble eightfold path is to be developed.
What is the noble eightfold path?

Here, monks, a monk develops right view dependent on seclusion... [and so on] ...he develops right concentration dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
Monks, for the direct knowledge, full understanding, exhaustion, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, this noble eightfold path is to be developed.
“Monks, there are these five higher fetters. Which five?
Lust for the realm of form, lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.”
“Monks, these are the five higher fetters.

which inclines toward Nibbāna, leans toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna."

This is the summary of the sections.
The first section is on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga);
the second is called the Abiding (Vihāra);
the third section is on Wrongness (Micchatta).
The fourth is by one who is practicing [the path] itself.
The fifth section concerns a member of another sect,
and the sixth concerns the sun.
The seventh chapter is on "Much Done," the eighth is on "Arising," and the ninth is the "Day" chapter.
The tenth is on heedfulness;
the eleventh is the Chapter on the Powers;
the twelfth in the text is on Searches.
The Flood Chapter consists of thirteen [discourses].
